title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and use Tamil kinship terms to address people.
intro:
Tamil kinship vocabulary is precise: there is no single word for 'brother' or 'sister' — you must say **elder** or **younger**. These words are also used to address strangers politely: a shopkeeper might be அண்ணா 'elder brother', an older woman அம்மா 'mother'.

Grammatically you will learn how to say *my, your, his* and how Tamil makes plurals.

vocab.en: mother; also polite address to any woman

vocab.note: addressed as அண்ணா aṇṇā — also used for any slightly older man

vocab.en: elder sister; also polite address to a young woman

vocab.note: 'a man' in speech is usually ஆம்பள āmbaḷa
also a friendly address for an older man
respectful/neutral நண்பர் naṇbar; spoken also ஃப்ரெண்ட் 'friend'

phrases.en: How many children do you have?
I have one son and one daughter.
Are you married? (lit. has your wedding happened?)
I have two elder brothers and one younger sister.
She is my mother's younger sister.

grammar.title: My, your, his: possessives
grammar.body:
Possessive pronouns go **before** the noun:

என் *en* — my (also என்னோட *ennōḍa*)
உன் *un* — your (informal) (உன்னோட *unnōḍa*)
உங்க *unga* — your (polite) (written உங்கள்)
அவனோட *avanōḍa* — his (informal)
அவளோட *avaḷōḍa* — her (informal)
அவரோட *avarōḍa* — his/her (respectful)
அவங்களோட *avangaḷōḍa* — their; her (respectful)
எங்க *enga* — our (not yours); நம்ம *namma* — our (yours too)

For nouns, add the spoken genitive **-ஓட** *-ōḍa* (written -உடைய *-uḍaiya* or -இன் *-in*): ரவியோட வீடு 'Ravi's house', அம்மாவோட தங்கச்சி 'mother's sister'. Note that Tamils say **நம்ம ஊரு** 'our town' warmly, even to strangers.

examples.en: Priya's elder brother is a doctor.

grammar.title: Plurals and 'gender' of nouns
grammar.body:
The plural suffix is **-கள்** *-kaḷ* (spoken usually **-ங்க** *-nga*): புத்தகம் → புத்தகங்கள் / புத்தகங்க 'books', குழந்தை → குழந்தைகள் / குழந்தைங்க 'children'. Nouns ending in -ம் change it to -ங்: மரம் → மரங்கள். After a long vowel or a two-syllable short word the k doubles: பூ → பூக்கள் 'flowers'.

Tamil nouns have no masculine/feminine for things. Instead grammar divides the world into **rational** beings (humans, gods) and **non-rational** (animals, things). Only rational beings get he/she verb endings; everything else is அது 'it'. With numbers and words like எல்லாம் the plural suffix is often left off in speech: ரெண்டு அண்ணன் 'two elder brothers'.

grammar.title: 'I have…' with family: dative + noun
grammar.body:
Tamil has no verb 'to have'. For relatives (and many other things) you put the owner in the **dative** case with **-க்கு** *-kku* and simply state what there is: **எனக்கு ரெண்டு தம்பி** 'to-me two younger-brothers' = 'I have two younger brothers'. You may add இருக்காங்க / இருக்காரு 'are there', but it is often left out.

Dative pronouns: எனக்கு *enakku* (to me), உனக்கு *unakku*, உங்களுக்கு *ungaḷukku*, அவனுக்கு *avanukku*, அவளுக்கு *avaḷukku*, அவருக்கு *avarukku*, அவங்களுக்கு *avangaḷukku*, எங்களுக்கு *engaḷukku*, நமக்கு *namakku*.

examples.en: I don't have a younger sister.

dialogue.title: Looking at the wedding album
dialogue.setting: Meena shows her colleague Sarah photos from her elder sister's wedding.

lines.speaker: Meena
lines.en: This is my elder sister's wedding.

lines.speaker: Meena
lines.native: அவங்க என் அம்மா. பக்கத்துல என் அப்பா.
lines.roman: avanga en ammā. pakkattula en appā.
lines.en: That's my mother. Next to her is my father.

lines.speaker: Meena
lines.native: அவன் என் தம்பி. அவனுக்குப் பதினஞ்சு வயசு.
lines.roman: avan en tambi. avanukkup padinanju vayasu.
lines.en: He's my younger brother. He's fifteen.

lines.speaker: Meena
lines.native: ஆமா! இவரு என் தாத்தா, இவங்க பாட்டி, இவங்க எல்லாரும் சொந்தக்காரங்க.
lines.roman: āmā! ivaru en tāttā, ivanga pāṭṭi, ivanga ellārum sondakkāranga.
lines.en: Yes! This is my grandfather, this my grandmother, and these are all relatives.

culture: Tamils use kinship words with almost everyone: a young shop assistant is தம்பி, a slightly older man அண்ணா, a woman of your age அக்கா, an older woman அம்மா or ஆன்ட்டி. Calling elders by their first name is impolite. Traditionally, cross-cousin marriage (a man marrying his மாமா's or அத்தை's daughter) was common, which is why மாமா means both 'mother's brother' and 'father-in-law'.

tip.title: My, your, his: before the noun
tip.body:
- Possessives go **before** the noun: **என்** அம்மா 'my mum', **உங்க** அப்பா 'your dad (polite)', **அவரோட** பேரு 'his name'.
- For a person's name or a noun, add **-ஓட**: டாமோட குடும்பம் 'Tom's family', அப்பாவோட பேரு 'Dad's name'.
- Don't confuse **என்** 'my' with **எனக்கு** 'to me'.

sentences.en: My parents live in Sri Lanka.

tip.title: 'I have…' is 'to me there is…'
tip.body:
- Tamil has no verb 'have'. Put the owner in the dative **-க்கு** and name what there is: **எனக்கு** ஒரு அக்கா 'I have an elder sister'.
- எனக்கு, **உங்களுக்கு**, **அவருக்கு**, **அவனுக்கு**…
- You can add இருக்காங்க / இருக்காரு; 'I don't have' is **எனக்கு … இல்ல**.
- There's no plain 'brother': say **அண்ணன்** (elder) or **தம்பி** (younger).

sentences.en: Do you have an elder sister?
I don't have a younger brother.
He has an elder sister and a younger brother.
My elder sister lives in Chennai.
How many brothers do you have?

tip.title: Plurals: -கள், spoken -ங்க
tip.body:
- The plural ending is **-கள்**, in speech usually **-ங்க**: குழந்தை → **குழந்தைங்க** 'children'.
- After a number the noun usually stays singular: ரெண்டு **பையன்** 'two sons'.
- People get he/she verbs; animals and things are அது 'it'.
- Boy is **பையன்**, girl is **பொண்ணு** (written பெண்).

sentences.en: Is it a boy or a girl? (a baby)

tip.title: Aunts and uncles have exact names
tip.body:
- Dad's side: **சித்தப்பா** (Dad's younger brother), **பெரியப்பா** (Dad's elder brother), **அத்தை** (Dad's sister). Mum's brother is **மாமா**.
- Whose relative: add **-ஓட**: அம்மா**வோட** தங்கச்சி.
- 'Are you married?' is 'has your wedding happened?': கல்யாணம் **ஆயிடுச்சா?** → ஆயிடுச்சு / இன்னும் **ஆகல** 'not yet'.

sentences.en: My māmā is my mum's younger brother.

tip.title: Family words for everyone
tip.body:
- Tamils address people with kinship words: a man a bit older than you is **அண்ணா**, a young man **தம்பி**, a woman your age **அக்கா**, an older woman **அம்மா**.
- Note the calling form: அண்ணன் → **அண்ணா!**
- Ask after the whole family with **எல்லாரும்** 'everyone'.

sentences.en: How are you, ma’am? (to an older woman)
What's your name? (to a young woman)

sentences.native: அவ என் தோழி இல்ல, என் தங்கச்சி.
sentences.roman: ava en tōḻi illa, en tangacchi.
sentences.en: She's not my friend, she's my younger sister.
